items.title: Foundation of the Empire & Chandragupta Maurya
items.body:
## Foundation of the Empire & Chandragupta Maurya

**In one line:** The Mauryan Empire was founded in 322 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nanda dynasty with his mentor Chanakya and built India's first all-India empire.

**Why it is asked:** The founder, the year, the mentor and the Seleucus deal are high-frequency single-fact questions, and the "first political unification of India" is a favourite statement line.

### The story
- Amid the power of the **Nanda dynasty**, a young **Chandragupta Maurya**, guided by his teacher **Chanakya (also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta)**, overthrew the last Nanda ruler **Dhanananda** in **322 BCE**.
- His origins are debated: **Brahmanical tradition** says he was born of a **shudra woman** in the Nanda court; **Buddhist tradition** links him to a **Kshatriya clan (the Mauryas)** of the **Gorakhpur** region.
- Result: for the **first time in Indian history** one empire united most of the subcontinent, and **monarchy** replaced the older republics and oligarchies.
- He then defeated the Greek general **Seleucus I in 305 BCE**, gaining **Afghanistan, Baluchistan and the land west of the Indus**, giving **500 war elephants** in return and receiving the ambassador **Megasthenes**.
- The empire covered **Bihar, Orissa, Bengal** and the **north and north-west**; only **Kerala, Tamil Nadu and parts of the North-East** stayed outside. An **autocrat**, he kept a huge army — **Pliny** records **600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants**. Capital: **Pataliputra** (modern **Patna**).

### Picture it
| Ruler | Rough dates | One defining fact |
|---|---|---|
| Chandragupta | 322–298 BCE | Founder; beat Seleucus (305 BCE) |
| Bindusara | 297–273 BCE | Extended empire southward |
| Ashoka | c. 268–232 BCE | Kalinga War; embraced Buddhism |

### Terms explained
- **Nanda dynasty** — the rulers of Magadha whom Chandragupta overthrew.
- **Chanakya / Kautilya / Vishnugupta** — three names for the same mentor-minister.
- **Autocrat** — a ruler who keeps all power in his own hands.

### Don't confuse
- **Chandragupta Maurya** (322 BCE founder) vs **Chandragupta I** of the much later Gupta dynasty (4th century CE).
- Chandragupta **gained** the north-west **from** Seleucus — he did not cede land to him.

**Remember it:** Ruler order "CBA" = Chandragupta → Bindusara → Ashoka, the three peak Mauryas.

**TL;DR**
- Founded 322 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya; mentor Chanakya; last Nanda was Dhanananda.
- Beat Seleucus I in 305 BCE: won the north-west for 500 elephants; got Megasthenes.
- First unification of India; capital Pataliputra; far south stayed outside.

keyPoints: Mauryan Empire founded in 322 BCE by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nanda ruler Dhanananda with Chanakya's help.
Defeated Seleucus I in 305 BCE, gaining Afghanistan/Baluchistan/west-of-Indus in exchange for 500 elephants.
Achieved the first political unification of India; monarchy replaced republics/oligarchies.
Kerala, Tamil Nadu and parts of the North-East remained outside Mauryan rule.
Pliny records his army as 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants.

items.title: Chanakya (Kautilya) & the Arthashastra
items.body:
## Chanakya (Kautilya) & the Arthashastra

**In one line:** Chanakya, the mentor of Chandragupta, wrote the Arthashastra — the single most important source on how the Mauryan state was run.

**Why it is asked:** Examiners love the three names of one man (Chanakya = Kautilya = Vishnugupta), the book's size (15 books, 180 chapters) and the welfare idea of Yogakshema.

### The story
- **Chanakya**, also called **Kautilya** and **Vishnugupta**, was the **contemporary and mentor** of Chandragupta and planned the overthrow of the Nandas.
- He stayed on as **prime minister** into the reign of **Bindusara**, so his influence outlived the founder.
- He wrote the **Arthashastra in Sanskrit** — a manual of statecraft with **15 books and 180 chapters** in **3 broad divisions**, covering law, administration, economics and military strategy.
- Its central idea is the king's duty of **Yogakshema (welfare)** — securing law and order plus **agriculture, irrigation, fair taxation and disaster relief**.
- Though the surviving text was **compiled some centuries later**, it preserves **authentic information** about Mauryan government.

### Picture it
| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Author | Kautilya (Chanakya / Vishnugupta) |
| Language | Sanskrit |
| Size | 15 books, 180 chapters, 3 divisions |
| Core idea | Yogakshema — welfare of the people |

### Terms explained
- **Arthashastra** — literally "the science of wealth/statecraft"; a treatise on running a kingdom.
- **Yogakshema** — the ruler's duty to secure the welfare and security of his subjects.

### Don't confuse
- **Arthashastra** (Kautilya, a treatise) vs **Indica** (Megasthenes, a foreigner's account) vs **Mudrarakshasa** (Vishakhadatta, a drama).

**Remember it:** Size hook — "15 books, 180 chapters" because 15 × 12 = 180.

**TL;DR**
- Chanakya = Kautilya = Vishnugupta; mentor of Chandragupta, minister under Bindusara too.
- Arthashastra: Sanskrit; 15 books, 180 chapters; the top source on Mauryan administration.
- Stresses Yogakshema (welfare); compiled later but authentic in detail.
keyPoints: Chanakya = Kautilya = Vishnugupta; mentor of Chandragupta and prime minister continuing under Bindusara.
Arthashastra was written by Kautilya in Sanskrit — the single most important source on the Mauryas.
Structure: 15 books, 180 chapters, 3 broad divisions.
Emphasises the king's duty of Yogakshema (welfare) via irrigation, fair taxation and disaster relief.
Compiled centuries later but contains authentic administrative detail.

items.title: Megasthenes' Indica & Literary Sources
items.body:
## Megasthenes' Indica & Literary Sources

**In one line:** Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador at Pataliputra, wrote Indica — the key foreign eyewitness source on Mauryan India, which survives only in fragments.

**Why it is asked:** The "who wrote Indica / whose ambassador was he" pair and the fact that Indica is lost (only fragments survive) are common traps.

### The story
- **Megasthenes** was the **Greek ambassador** sent by **Seleucus** to **Chandragupta's court** at **Pataliputra**.
- He recorded Mauryan society, administration and the capital in a book called **Indica**; the original is **lost** and survives only as **fragments quoted by later Greek writers**.
- Other sources fill the picture: the **Arthashastra** (Kautilya) is the foremost administrative source; the Sanskrit drama **Mudrarakshasa** by **Vishakhadatta** (Gupta era) dramatises **Chandragupta's victory over the Nandas**; and **Buddhist literature and the Puranas** add dynastic and religious detail.

### Picture it
| Source | By whom | What it gives |
|---|---|---|
| Indica | Megasthenes (Greek) | Outsider's view of court and society |
| Arthashastra | Kautilya | Insider's manual of administration |
| Mudrarakshasa | Vishakhadatta | Drama on fall of the Nandas |

### Terms explained
- **Indica** — Megasthenes' Greek account of Mauryan India.
- **Fragments** — short passages preserved only because later writers quoted them; the whole book is gone.

### Don't confuse
- **Megasthenes** (wrote Indica) vs **Kautilya** (wrote the Arthashastra) vs **Vishakhadatta** (wrote Mudrarakshasa).

**Remember it:** Two pillars of Mauryan sources — "A and I": Arthashastra (insider Kautilya) and Indica (outsider Megasthenes).

**TL;DR**
- Megasthenes = Seleucus's envoy to Chandragupta at Pataliputra; wrote Indica.
- Indica survives only as fragments in later Greek writers.
- Supporting sources: Arthashastra, Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta), Buddhist texts and Puranas.
keyPoints: Megasthenes was Seleucus's ambassador to Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra.
He wrote Indica; the original is lost and survives only as fragments in later Greek writers.
Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta, Gupta era) dramatises Chandragupta's defeat of the Nandas under Kautilya.
Buddhist texts and the Puranas supplement the sources.
Together with the Arthashastra, Indica is a key window into Mauryan administration.
items.mnemonic: Two pillars of Mauryan sources — 'A & I': Arthashastra (insider Kautilya) + Indica (outsider Megasthenes).

items.title: Bindusara (297–272/268 BCE)
items.body:
## Bindusara (297–272/268 BCE)

**In one line:** Bindusara, Chandragupta's son, extended the Mauryan empire into the south and was known to the Greeks as the "slayer of enemies".

**Why it is asked:** His accession year (297 BCE), his Greek title Amitragata, and the fact that Kalinga stayed unconquered until Ashoka are the usual question hooks.

### The story
- **Bindusara**, the **son and successor of Chandragupta**, took the throne in **297 BCE**.
- The Greeks called him **Amitragata / Amitrochates**, meaning **"slayer of enemies"**.
- He **pushed the empire southward**, bringing **sixteen states** under Mauryan control across much of the **peninsula**.
- Apart from the far south, the only kingdom left outside was **Kalinga** — later conquered by **Ashoka**.
- His reign kept up **links with the Greeks**, and **Kautilya continued as prime minister**.

### Picture it
| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Accession | 297 BCE |
| Greek title | Amitragata — "slayer of enemies" |
| Expansion | 16 states of the peninsula |
| Left unconquered | Kalinga (Ashoka later took it) |

### Terms explained
- **Amitragata** — Greek rendering of a title meaning "slayer of foes".
- **Peninsula** — the southern, triangular part of India jutting into the sea.

### Don't confuse
- **Bindusara** conquered much of the south but **not Kalinga**; **Ashoka** conquered Kalinga.

**Remember it:** Bindusara the "enemy-slayer" (Amitragata) slew sixteen states but not Kalinga.

**TL;DR**
- Son of Chandragupta; throne in 297 BCE.
- Greeks called him Amitragata ("slayer of enemies"); brought 16 states under rule.
- Kalinga stayed unconquered until Ashoka; Kautilya stayed on as minister.
keyPoints: Bindusara, son of Chandragupta, ascended in 297 BCE.
Greeks called him Amitragata / Amitrochates — 'slayer of enemies'.
Extended the empire south, subduing sixteen states across the peninsula.
Kalinga remained unconquered until Ashoka's reign.
Kautilya continued as prime minister; Greek links were maintained.
items.mnemonic: Bindusara = 'Amitraghata, the enemy-slayer' — he slew 16 states but not Kalinga.

items.title: Ashoka — Accession & Inscriptions
items.body:
## Ashoka — Accession & Inscriptions

**In one line:** Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta, was the first Indian ruler to speak directly to his people through stone inscriptions scattered across the subcontinent and beyond.

**Why it is asked:** The number of inscriptions (39), the title "Devanampiya Piyadasi", the sites that reveal his real name (Maski), and where the pillars were quarried (Chunar) are repeat exam points.

### The story
- **Ashoka**, **son of Bindusara**, ascended around **268 BCE** and is counted among the greatest rulers of the subcontinent.
- He was the **first ruler to keep direct contact with his people** through **inscriptions** carved on rocks and pillars.
- There are **39 Ashokan inscriptions**, grouped as **Major Rock, Minor Rock, Separate Rock, Major Pillar and Minor Pillar edicts**.
- His **personal name "Ashoka"** appears only in the **Maski Edict** and copies of **Minor Rock Edict I** (three sites in Karnataka, one in Madhya Pradesh); everywhere else he is called **"Devanampiya Piyadasi"** (Beloved-of-the-Gods).
- Stone **pillars were quarried at Chunar near Varanasi**, each a **single piece of buff-coloured sandstone**, then carried across India. Inscriptions are found in **India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan**, usually along **ancient highways**. The **Kanganahalli** site (Karnataka) yielded a **"Ranyo Ashoka"** portrait-inscription of the emperor.

### Picture it
| Clue | What it tells us |
|---|---|
| "Devanampiya Piyadasi" | The usual title in the edicts |
| Maski / Minor Rock Edict I | The few places giving the name "Ashoka" |
| Chunar sandstone | Where the pillars were quarried |

### Terms explained
- **Edict** — an official order of the ruler, here carved in stone.
- **Devanampiya Piyadasi** — "Beloved-of-the-Gods, of pleasing countenance", Ashoka's inscription title.

### Don't confuse
- The title **Devanampiya Piyadasi** is used almost everywhere; the actual name **Ashoka** appears only at Maski and Minor Rock Edict I sites.

**Remember it:** "MASKI unmasks Ashoka" — only Maski and Minor Rock Edict I give his real name.

**TL;DR**
- Son of Bindusara; throne c. 268 BCE; first ruler to address people via inscriptions.
- 39 inscriptions; usually titled Devanampiya Piyadasi; real name only at Maski etc.
- Pillars quarried at Chunar; edicts in India, Nepal, Pakistan, Afghanistan.
keyPoints: Ashoka, son of Bindusara, ascended c. 268 BCE (272/268); first Indian ruler to speak to his people via inscriptions.
39 inscriptions: Major/Minor Rock, Separate Rock, Major/Minor Pillar edicts.
Name 'Ashoka' appears only in the Maski Edict and Minor Rock Edict I; elsewhere he is 'Devanampiya Piyadasi'.
Pillars quarried at Chunar (near Varanasi); each is a single piece of buff sandstone.
Edicts found in India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan, placed along ancient highways.
Kanganahalli (Sannati, Karnataka) yielded the 'Ranyo Ashoka' portrait-inscription of the emperor.
items.mnemonic: Ashoka's name-clue — 'MASKI unmasks Ashoka' (only Maski/Minor Rock Edict I give his real name).

items.title: The Kalinga War (261 BCE) & Its Impact
items.body:
## The Kalinga War (261 BCE) & Its Impact

**In one line:** The Kalinga War of 261 BCE was so bloody that it turned Ashoka from a conqueror into a preacher of peace who embraced Buddhism.

**Why it is asked:** The war year (261 BCE), the edict that records it (13th Major Rock Edict) and the shift from Bherighosha to Dhammaghosha are classic cause-and-effect questions.

### The story
- **Cause:** Ashoka attacked **Kalinga** (coastal Odisha) in **261 BCE**; the conquest caused enormous **loss of life**.
- **Event/record:** the **Thirteenth Major Rock Edict** describes the war and Ashoka's **remorse**; the separate **Kalinga Edict** proclaims **"All men are my children."**
- **Result:** Ashoka **embraced Buddhism** and switched from **physical conquest to cultural conquest** — tradition sums this up as moving from **Bherighosha (the war-drum)** to **Dhammaghosha (the drum of dhamma)**.
- He framed **state policy on Buddhist principles**, sent **ambassadors of peace** to Greece and West Asia, and dispatched his children **Mahinda (Mahendra) and Sanghamitra to Ceylon (Sri Lanka)**.

### Picture it
```
Before Kalinga        After Kalinga
war-drum  ───────▶    drum of dhamma
Bherighosha           Dhammaghosha
conquest by army      conquest by ideas
```

### Terms explained
- **Bherighosha** — "sound of the war-drum", the policy of military conquest.
- **Dhammaghosha** — "sound of dhamma", the policy of winning people by moral teaching.

### Don't confuse
- **Kalinga War = 261 BCE** (not 305 BCE, which is the Seleucus war; not 232 BCE, Ashoka's death).

**Remember it:** Kalinga's aftermath = "Bheri to Dhamma" — the war-drum falls silent for the drum of dhamma.

**TL;DR**
- Kalinga War fought 261 BCE; recorded in the 13th Major Rock Edict.
- Its bloodshed made Ashoka embrace Buddhism and non-violence.
- Shift from Bherighosha (war) to Dhammaghosha (dhamma); missions sent to Sri Lanka.
keyPoints: Kalinga War fought in 261 BCE; its bloodshed transformed Ashoka.
13th Major Rock Edict records the Kalinga war; the Kalinga Edict declares 'All men are my children'.
Shift from Bherighosha (war-drum) to Dhammaghosha (dhamma) — physical to cultural conquest.
Ashoka embraced Buddhism and promoted non-violence.
Sent his children Mahendra (Mahinda) and Sanghamitra to Ceylon/Sri Lanka.
items.mnemonic: Kalinga aftermath = 'Bheri to Dhamma' — the war-drum (Bherighosha) falls silent for the drum of dhamma (Dhammaghosha).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Impact of the Kalinga War)

items.title: Ashoka's Dhamma & Internal Policy
items.body:
## Ashoka's Dhamma & Internal Policy

**In one line:** Dhamma was Ashoka's code of moral governance — not a new religion — spread through special officers and backed by the ideal of the king as a father to his people.

**Why it is asked:** The nature of Dhamma (moral, not sectarian), the officers who spread it (Dhamma Mahamatras) and the Rajukas' powers are regularly tested.

### The story
- After Kalinga, Ashoka launched **Dhamma**, stressing **moral conduct, social welfare and respect for all living beings** — a broad ethical code, not a single sect.
- He set the ideal of **paternal kingship**: the king treating his **subjects as his children**.
- He appointed **Dhamma Mahamatras** — officers who **propagated dharma** and looked after the **material well-being** of common people, including women.
- He appointed **Rajukas**, officers empowered **both to reward and to punish** people, and told the mahamatras **not to torture people without due cause** — a welfare-minded rule.

### Picture it
| Officer | Job |
|---|---|
| Dhamma Mahamatra | Spread dhamma; secure people's welfare |
| Rajuka | Reward and punish; later land assessment |

### Terms explained
- **Dhamma** — Ashoka's code of ethical living and good governance (from Sanskrit "dharma").
- **Paternal kingship** — the idea that the ruler cares for subjects as a father cares for children.
- **Dhamma Mahamatra** — a special officer created to teach and oversee Dhamma.

### Don't confuse
- **Dhamma** is a moral code for all; it is **not** the same as formally converting the empire to Buddhism.

**Remember it:** Dhamma officers — "Mahamatras Mind morals, Rajukas Reward and Rebuke".

**TL;DR**
- Dhamma = moral governance, welfare and respect for all life (not a sect).
- Paternal kingship — subjects treated as the king's children.
- Spread by Dhamma Mahamatras; Rajukas could reward and punish.
keyPoints: Dhamma stressed moral governance, social welfare and respect for all life.
Ashoka set the ideal of paternal kingship — subjects treated as his children.
Dhamma Mahamatras propagated dharma and looked after people's material well-being.
Rajukas were empowered both to reward and to punish.
Teachings targeted all groups including women and reinforced the family/social order.
items.mnemonic: Dhamma officers — 'Mahamatras Mind morals, Rajukas Reward & Rebuke.'

items.title: The Edicts of Ashoka — Rock & Pillar Edicts
items.body:
## The Edicts of Ashoka — Rock & Pillar Edicts

**In one line:** Ashoka's edicts are inscriptions on rocks and pillars that record his orders on dhamma, welfare and events like the Kalinga War.

**Why it is asked:** Edict-to-content matching (which edict says what) is one of the most common Mauryan question formats.

### The story
- The **Major Rock Edicts** are a set of **14** detailed rock inscriptions. Key ones:
  - **First Rock Edict** — bans **animal sacrifices**.
  - **Fourth Rock Edict** — **Bherighosha replaced by Dhammaghosha**.
  - **Fifth Rock Edict** — **appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras**.
  - **Thirteenth Rock Edict** — describes the **Kalinga War (261 BCE)**.
- Among the **Pillar Edicts**: **Pillar Edict V** lists **animals not to be killed** and records the **release of 25 prisoners**; **Pillar Edict VI** deals with the **Dhamma policy**.
- Special inscriptions: the **Rummindei Inscription (Nepal)** marks the **Buddha's birthplace at Lumbini**; the **Sohgaura Copper Plate** records **famine relief in Magadha**; the **Kalinga Edict** declares **"All men are my children."**
- The **Ashoka Chakra** on the Lion Capital shows the **Dharma Chakra** with **24 spokes**. **Erragudi (Yerragudi) in Andhra Pradesh** carries Major Rock Edicts — a key AP site.

### Picture it
| Edict | Message |
|---|---|
| 1st Rock Edict | Ban on animal sacrifice |
| 4th Rock Edict | Bherighosha → Dhammaghosha |
| 5th Rock Edict | Appoints Dhamma Mahamatras |
| 13th Rock Edict | Kalinga War |

### Terms explained
- **Rock Edict** — an edict carved on a rock surface; **Pillar Edict** — one carved on a free-standing pillar.
- **Rummindei Inscription** — the pillar inscription at Lumbini marking the Buddha's birthplace.

### Don't confuse
- The **1st Rock Edict** bans sacrifice; the **13th** records Kalinga — do not swap them.
- Buddha's birthplace is marked by the **Rummindei** inscription, not the First Rock Edict.

**Remember it:** Rock Edicts "1-4-5-13" = Sacrifice-ban, Drum-swap, Mahamatras, Kalinga.

**TL;DR**
- 14 Major Rock Edicts; 1st bans sacrifice, 4th drum-swap, 5th mahamatras, 13th Kalinga.
- Pillar Edict V: animals + release of 25 prisoners; Pillar Edict VI: Dhamma policy.
- Rummindei (Nepal) marks Lumbini; Erragudi (AP) is a major-rock-edict site.
keyPoints: Major Edicts = 14 rock inscriptions.
1st RE: bans animal sacrifice; 4th RE: Bherighosha → Dhammaghosha; 5th RE: appoints Dhamma Mahamatras; 13th RE: Kalinga War.
Pillar Edict V: animals not to be killed + release of 25 prisoners; Pillar Edict VI: Dhamma policy.
Rummindei (Nepal) marks the Buddha's birthplace (Lumbini); Saugara copper plate records famine relief.
Ashoka Chakra = Dharma Chakra with 24 spokes.
Erragudi (Yerragudi) in Andhra Pradesh bears Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts — a key AP Ashokan site.
items.mnemonic: Rock Edicts '1-4-5-13' = Sacrifice-ban, Drum-swap, Mahamatras, Kalinga.

items.title: Languages & Scripts of the Edicts
items.body:
## Languages & Scripts of the Edicts

**In one line:** Ashoka's edicts were written in different languages and scripts depending on the region — Brahmi across most of India, Kharoshthi in the north-west, and Greek/Aramaic in Afghanistan.

**Why it is asked:** Region-to-script matching (Brahmi vs Kharoshthi vs Greek/Aramaic) is a frequent, easily-confused question.

### The story
- The **languages** used were **Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic**.
- Across **most of the subcontinent** the edicts are in **Prakrit written in the Brahmi script**.
- In the **north-west**, they are in the **Aramaic language and Kharoshthi script** — the **Shahbazgarhi and Manshera** edicts are in **Kharoshthi**.
- In **Afghanistan**, edicts appear in **both Aramaic and Greek** (for example the Kandahar bilingual edict).

### Picture it
| Region | Language | Script |
|---|---|---|
| Most of India | Prakrit | Brahmi |
| North-west | Aramaic | Kharoshthi |
| Afghanistan | Aramaic and Greek | Aramaic and Greek |

### Terms explained
- **Script** — the set of written signs used to record a language (how it looks on stone).
- **Brahmi** — the main ancient Indian script, ancestor of most Indian scripts today.
- **Kharoshthi** — a script used only in the north-west, written right-to-left.

### Don't confuse
- **Language** (Prakrit, Greek, Aramaic) is not the same as **script** (Brahmi, Kharoshthi, Greek, Aramaic).

**Remember it:** Scripts by direction — "Brahmi Broadly, Kharoshthi in the (north-)West".

**TL;DR**
- Languages: Prakrit, Greek, Aramaic.
- Most of India: Prakrit in Brahmi; north-west: Aramaic in Kharoshthi (Shahbazgarhi, Manshera).
- Afghanistan: both Aramaic and Greek.
keyPoints: Languages of the edicts: Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic.
Most of India: Prakrit language in Brahmi script.
North-west: Aramaic language, Kharoshthi script (Shahbazgarhi and Manshera).
Afghanistan: both Aramaic and Greek.
Brahmi is the dominant script; Kharoshthi is confined to the north-west.
items.mnemonic: Scripts by direction — 'Brahmi Broadly, Kharoshthi in the (north-)West'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (languages/scripts of edicts)

items.title: Ashoka & the Spread of Buddhism
items.body:
## Ashoka & the Spread of Buddhism

**In one line:** Ashoka turned Buddhism from a regional faith into a world religion by hosting the Third Buddhist Council and sending missionaries abroad.

**Why it is asked:** The Third Council (venue, patron, president) and the missionaries to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitra) are repeat facts.

### The story
- Ashoka became a **major patron of Buddhism**, helping it spread across **Asia, including Sri Lanka**.
- The **Third Buddhist Council** met under his patronage in **250 BCE at Pataliputra**, presided over by **Mogaliputta Tissa**, to **purify the Sangha** of corrupt and opportunistic factions.
- He sent missionaries — including his son **Mahinda (Mahendra)** and daughter **Sanghamitra** — to **Ceylon (Sri Lanka)**, and others to **Burma** and beyond.
- Because of this outreach, Ashoka is called the **"First Global Ambassador of India"**, linking the developed Gangetic basin with outlying regions and the wider world.

### Picture it
| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Council | Third Buddhist Council |
| Place / year | Pataliputra, 250 BCE |
| President | Mogaliputta Tissa |
| Missionaries | Mahinda (son), Sanghamitra (daughter) to Sri Lanka |

### Terms explained
- **Sangha** — the community of Buddhist monks.
- **Buddhist Council** — a gathering of monks to settle doctrine and discipline.

### Don't confuse
- The **Third Council** (Pataliputra, Mogaliputta Tissa) under **Ashoka** is different from the **Fourth Council** (Kashmir, under Kanishka).

**Remember it:** Third Council = "3 P's" — Pataliputra, Presided by Mogaliputta Tissa, to Purify the Sangha.

**TL;DR**
- Ashoka spread Buddhism across Asia, including Sri Lanka.
- Third Buddhist Council: 250 BCE, Pataliputra, under Mogaliputta Tissa, to purify the Sangha.
- Missionaries Mahinda and Sanghamitra went to Ceylon; Ashoka = "First Global Ambassador of India".
keyPoints: Ashoka was a major patron of Buddhism, spreading it across Asia including Sri Lanka.
Third Buddhist Council: 250 BC at Pataliputra, presided by Mogaliputta Tissa.
Council aimed to purify the Sangha of corruption and factions.
Missionaries Mahinda (son) and Sanghamitra (daughter) went to Ceylon; others to Burma.
Ashoka is called the 'First Global Ambassador of India'.
The Third Buddhist Council (Pataliputra) was convened under Ashoka and presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa.
items.mnemonic: 3rd Council = '3 P's' — Pataliputra, Presided by Mogaliputta Tissa, to Purify the Sangha.

items.title: Mauryan Central Administration
items.body:
## Mauryan Central Administration

**In one line:** The Mauryan state was an autocratic monarchy run by a king, a council of advisers and a set of specialised high officers for revenue, justice and the army.

**Why it is asked:** Officer-to-function matching (Samaharta, Sannidhata, Vyavaharika, Pradeshta) and the "advice not binding" point are common statement questions.

### The story
- Power was **concentrated in the king**, yet he was **assisted by a council whose advice was not binding**; the top officers were chosen from the councillors.
- Our knowledge comes mainly from **Megasthenes' Indica** and **Kautilya's Arthashastra**.
- The highest functionaries (**tirthas**) were the **Mantrin** (minister), **Purohita** (chief priest), **Senapati** (commander-in-chief) and **Yuvaraja** (crown prince).
- Specialised officers from the Arthashastra: **Samaharta** (collector-general of revenue, head of assessment), **Sannidhata** (chief treasurer and keeper of the storehouse), **Vyavaharika** (chief justice of the **civil** court) and **Pradeshta** (chief justice of the **criminal** court).
- An **elaborate system of spies** supported the whole machinery, and Ashoka later added the **Dhamma Mahamatra** post.

### Picture it
| Officer | Function |
|---|---|
| Mantrin / Purohita / Senapati | Minister / priest / army chief |
| Samaharta | Revenue assessment (collector-general) |
| Sannidhata | Treasury and storehouse |
| Vyavaharika / Pradeshta | Civil / criminal chief justice |

### Terms explained
- **Tirthas** — the highest category of state officers.
- **Samaharta** — the chief revenue officer in charge of assessment.
- **Sannidhata** — the chief treasury officer.

### Don't confuse
- **Samaharta** collects/assesses revenue; **Sannidhata** stores it in the treasury.
- **Vyavaharika** = civil court; **Pradeshta** = criminal court.

**Remember it:** Money officers "SS" — Samaharta collects (assessment), Sannidhata stores (treasury).

**TL;DR**
- Autocratic monarchy; council advisory (not binding); sources = Indica and Arthashastra.
- Tirthas: Mantrin, Purohita, Senapati, Yuvaraja.
- Samaharta (revenue), Sannidhata (treasury), Vyavaharika (civil), Pradeshta (criminal); spies backed the system.
keyPoints: Autocratic monarchy; king assisted by a council whose advice was non-binding.
Sources: Megasthenes' Indica and Kautilya's Arthashastra.
Tirthas: Mantrin (minister), Purohita (priest), Senapati (C-in-C), Yuvaraja (crown prince).
Samaharta = revenue collector-general/assessment; Sannidhata = chief treasurer.
Vyavaharika = civil court chief justice; Pradeshta = criminal court chief justice; espionage backed the system.
items.mnemonic: Money officers 'SS' — Samaharta collects (assessment), Sannidhata stores (treasury).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Features of administration; functionaries; officials)

items.title: Provincial, Local & Municipal Administration
items.body:
## Provincial, Local & Municipal Administration

**In one line:** Below the king, the empire was split into prince-governed provinces, with district and village officers, and a famous six-committee system running the capital Pataliputra.

**Why it is asked:** Province-to-capital matching and the "six committees of five members each" fact (from Megasthenes) are high-frequency.

### The story
- The empire was **divided into provinces**, each placed **under a prince** with the help of officials.
- Major provinces and capitals: **Uttarapatha → Taxila**, **Dakshinapatha → Suvarnagiri**, **Avantiratha → Ujjain**, **Eastern India → Tosali**, and **Kalinga → Tosali/Dhauli**.
- District and local officers: **Rashtrapala / Kumara** (viceroys over a province), **Pradesika** (like a district magistrate), **Rajukas** (surveying and land assessment, like Patwaris), **Yukta** (subordinate revenue officer), **Sthanika** (collecting officer) and **Gopa** (in charge of accounts).
- Per **Megasthenes**, the capital **Pataliputra** was run by **six committees of five members each**, with **separate arrangements for rural and urban** administration.

### Picture it
| Province | Capital |
|---|---|
| Uttarapatha | Taxila |
| Dakshinapatha | Suvarnagiri |
| Avantiratha | Ujjain |
| Eastern India | Tosali |

### Terms explained
- **Kumara / Rashtrapala** — a royal prince serving as provincial viceroy.
- **Pradesika** — a district-level officer, roughly a district magistrate.
- **Rajuka** — officer for land survey and assessment (compare the later Patwari).

### Don't confuse
- **Taxila** was the capital of the **north** (Uttarapatha); **Suvarnagiri** of the **south** (Dakshinapatha) — do not swap.

**Remember it:** Pataliputra municipality = "6 × 5" — six committees, five members each (Megasthenes).

**TL;DR**
- Provinces under princes (Kumara/Rashtrapala): Taxila, Suvarnagiri, Ujjain, Tosali.
- District/local: Pradesika (magistrate), Rajukas (survey), Gopa (accounts).
- Pataliputra run by six committees of five members each (Megasthenes).

figure.alt: Map of the Maurya Empire showing the capital Pataliputra, provincial cities, edicts of Ashoka and Buddhist sites
figure.caption: The Maurya Empire at its height — capital Pataliputra with provincial centres such as Taxila, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri and Tosali, and sites of Ashoka's edicts.

keyPoints: Empire divided into provinces, each under a prince (Rashtrapala/Kumara as viceroy).
Provincial capitals: Uttarapatha–Taxila, Dakshinapatha–Suvarnagiri, Avantiratha–Ujjain, Kalinga–Tosali/Dhauli.
Pradesika ≈ district magistrate; Rajukas did land survey/assessment; Gopa kept accounts.
Pataliputra was run by six committees of five members each (Megasthenes).
Separate machinery existed for rural and urban administration.
items.mnemonic: Pataliputra municipality = '6 × 5' — six committees, five members each (Megasthenes).

items.title: Economy & Taxation
items.body:
## Economy & Taxation

**In one line:** The Mauryan economy was heavily state-controlled, with 27 superintendents, a land tax of one-fourth to one-sixth, state monopolies and punch-marked silver coins.

**Why it is asked:** The land-tax range, the "27 adhyakshas", the monopolies and the coin type are common factual and statement questions.

### The story
- The **state controlled all economic activity**, brought **new land under cultivation**, and ran **state farms** worked by **slaves and hired labour**.
- **27 superintendents (adhyakshas)** regulated the different economic activities.
- The **land tax** ranged from **one-fourth to one-sixth of the produce**, with extra cultivation demanded in emergencies; taxes were also collected **in kind**.
- **Samaharta** headed **assessment**, **Sannidhata** kept the **treasury and storehouse** — assessment mattered more than storage.
- The state held **monopolies over mining, the sale of liquor and the manufacture of arms**. The currency was **punch-marked silver coins** bearing symbols such as the **peacock and hill-crescent**.

### Picture it
| Head | Detail |
|---|---|
| Land tax | One-fourth to one-sixth of produce |
| Regulators | 27 adhyakshas (superintendents) |
| Monopolies | Mining, liquor, arms |
| Coins | Punch-marked silver (peacock, hill-crescent) |

### Terms explained
- **Adhyaksha** — a superintendent in charge of one branch of the economy.
- **Punch-marked coins** — early coins stamped with small symbols rather than a single design.
- **In kind** — paid as goods (grain, produce) instead of money.

### Don't confuse
- Land tax was **one-fourth to one-sixth** — not a flat one-sixth only.

**Remember it:** Tax slab "1/4 to 1/6" and monopolies "MLA" — Mining, Liquor, Arms.

**TL;DR**
- State-controlled economy; 27 adhyakshas regulate it.
- Land tax one-fourth to one-sixth; taxes also in kind.
- Monopolies on mining, liquor and arms; currency = punch-marked silver coins.
keyPoints: State controlled all economic activity; 27 adhyakshas (superintendents) regulated it.
Land tax: one-fourth to one-sixth of produce; extra cultivation demanded in emergencies.
Samaharta headed assessment; Sannidhata kept the treasury/storehouse; taxes also collected in kind.
State monopolies: mining, liquor sale, and manufacture of arms.
Currency: punch-marked silver coins with peacock and hill-crescent symbols.
items.mnemonic: Tax slab '1/4 to 1/6' and monopolies 'MLA' — Mining, Liquor, Arms.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Features of the Economy)

items.title: Art & Architecture
items.body:
## Art & Architecture

**In one line:** Mauryan art is famous for its highly polished monolithic sandstone pillars — crowned by the Sarnath Lion Capital, now India's national emblem — and the earliest rock-cut caves.

**Why it is asked:** The Lion Capital/national emblem, the single-stone polished pillars, and the Barabar caves (earliest rock-cut) are repeat facts.

### The story
- The Mauryans introduced **stone masonry on a wide scale** and achieved a **high polish** on stone.
- Each **pillar** was carved from a **single piece of buff-coloured sandstone**.
- The **Lion Capital of Ashoka** (from **Sarnath**) is **India's national emblem**; the **Ashoka Chakra** on it shows the Dharma Chakra with **24 spokes**.
- Artisans began **cutting caves out of rock for monks** — the earliest being the **Barabar caves near Gaya** (and the **Lomasrishi cave** in the same hills).
- Other surviving pieces: an **Ashokan pillar at Lauriya Nandangarh (Bihar)** and the **Bull capital at Rampurva**.

### Picture it
| Work | Place / note |
|---|---|
| Lion Capital | Sarnath — national emblem; chakra with 24 spokes |
| Bull capital | Rampurva |
| Earliest rock-cut caves | Barabar (near Gaya) |
| Pillar | Lauriya Nandangarh (Bihar) |

### Terms explained
- **Capital** (in art) — the carved top piece of a pillar (here, lions or a bull).
- **Monolithic** — made from a single block of stone.
- **Rock-cut cave** — a cave carved directly into solid rock.

### Don't confuse
- The **Lion Capital** is from **Sarnath**; the **Bull capital** is from **Rampurva** — do not swap the sites.

**Remember it:** Mauryan art "PPC" — Polished Pillars (single sandstone) and rock-cut Caves at Barabar.

**TL;DR**
- Large-scale stone masonry with a high polish; each pillar a single sandstone block.
- Lion Capital (Sarnath) = national emblem; chakra has 24 spokes.
- Earliest rock-cut caves at Barabar; Bull capital at Rampurva.

figure.alt: A tall polished Ashokan sandstone pillar topped by an animal capital
figure.caption: A monolithic Ashokan pillar with an animal capital (e.g., Lauriya Nandangarh, Bihar) — carved from a single piece of polished buff sandstone.

keyPoints: Mauryans introduced large-scale stone masonry with a distinctive high polish.
Each pillar was a single monolith of buff-coloured sandstone.
The Lion Capital of Ashoka (Sarnath) is India's national emblem; its chakra has 24 spokes.
Earliest rock-cut caves: Barabar caves near Gaya (also Lomasrishi caves).
Notable pieces: Ashokan pillar at Lauriya Nandangarh and the Bull capital at Rampurva.
items.mnemonic: Mauryan art 'PPC' — Polished Pillars (single sandstone), and rock-cut Caves at Barabar.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Art and Architecture; cultural elements)

items.title: Society & Material Culture
items.body:
## Society & Material Culture

**In one line:** Mauryan rule spread a new material culture — iron tools, writing, coins and fine NBPW pottery — out from the Gangetic core across much of India.

**Why it is asked:** The "firsts" (burnt bricks, ring-wells) and the hallmark NBPW pottery are common statement questions, often with a false "unaware of iron" trap.

### The story
- Mauryan conquest **opened the doors to trade and missionary activity**, carrying material culture beyond the Gangetic heartland.
- This culture rested on the **intensive use of iron**, the **spread of writing**, abundant **punch-marked coins**, fine **Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW)** pottery, **burnt bricks** and **ring wells**.
- Tools of the age included **socketed axes, sickles and ploughshares**, and the **spoked wheel** came into use.
- Firsts: **burnt bricks** were used for the **first time in north-eastern India**, and **ring-wells first appeared in the Gangetic plains** in this period. Ashoka also set a **high ideal of paternal kingship**, strengthening family and social order.

### Picture it
| Hallmark | Note |
|---|---|
| NBPW pottery | Fine glossy black ware of the period |
| Iron tools | Axes, sickles, ploughshares |
| Burnt bricks | First used in north-east India |
| Ring wells | First appear in the Gangetic plains |

### Terms explained
- **NBPW (Northern Black Polished Ware)** — a shiny, fine black pottery that marks the period.
- **Ring well** — a well lined with stacked pottery rings, used for water or drainage.

### Don't confuse
- The Mauryans **used iron intensively** — the statement that they were "unacquainted with iron" is false.

**Remember it:** Mauryan material culture "NBPW + BR" — NBPW pottery, Burnt bricks, Ring-wells.

**TL;DR**
- Trade and missions spread material culture out of the Gangetic core.
- Hallmarks: iron tools, writing, punch-marked coins, NBPW pottery, burnt bricks, ring wells.
- Firsts: burnt bricks in north-east India; ring-wells in the Gangetic plains.
keyPoints: Mauryan expansion spread material culture via trade and missionaries.
Hallmarks: intensive iron use, writing, punch-marked coins, NBPW pottery, burnt bricks, ring wells.
Tools: socketed axes, sickles, ploughshares; the spoked wheel came into use.
Burnt bricks used for the first time in north-eastern India in this period.
Ring-wells first appeared in the Gangetic plains during Mauryan times.
items.mnemonic: Mauryan material culture 'NBPW + BR' — NBPW pottery, Burnt bricks, Ring-wells.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Spread of material culture)

items.title: Decline & Successors of the Empire
items.body:
## Decline & Successors of the Empire

**In one line:** After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE the empire weakened under feeble successors and ended in 185 BCE when the last emperor Brihadratha was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga.

**Why it is asked:** The decline anchors (232 BCE death, 185 BCE assassination, Brihadratha, Pushyamitra Shunga) and the multiple debated causes are both prelims and mains favourites.

### The story
- The empire began to **break up after Ashoka's death in 232 BCE**, weakened by weak successors.
- The last emperor, **Brihadratha**, was **assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE**, ending the dynasty and starting the **Shunga** line.
- Later Mauryas (genealogy): **Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha**.
- Debated causes of decline:
  1. **Brahmanical reaction** — the ban on animal sacrifice hurt the priestly class economically.
  2. **Financial crisis** — a huge army and bureaucracy plus lavish grants to monks drained the treasury (gold images were later melted).
  3. **Oppressive rule** in outlying provinces (Taxila complaints).
  4. **Spread of material knowledge** — the Gangetic core lost its edge as new powers (Shungas, Kanvas, Chetis) rose.
  5. **Neglect of the North-West frontier** — unguarded passes before Scythian, Shaka and Greek incursions.

### Picture it
| Anchor | Date |
|---|---|
| Ashoka's death | 232 BCE |
| Brihadratha assassinated | 185 BCE |

### Terms explained
- **Brihadratha** — the last Mauryan emperor.
- **Pushyamitra Shunga** — the general who killed Brihadratha and founded the Shunga dynasty.
- **Brahmanical reaction** — resentment of the priestly class at Ashoka's anti-sacrifice policy.

### Don't confuse
- The empire ends in **185 BCE** (Brihadratha killed), while Ashoka died earlier in **232 BCE** — two different dates.

**Remember it:** Decline causes "BFONS" — Brahmanical reaction, Financial crisis, Oppression, New knowledge, North-west neglect.

**TL;DR**
- Decline began after Ashoka's death (232 BCE); dynasty ended 185 BCE.
- Brihadratha killed by Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded the Shunga dynasty.
- Causes: Brahmanical reaction, financial crisis, oppression, knowledge diffusion, frontier neglect.
keyPoints: Decline began after Ashoka's death in 232 BCE amid weak successors.
Last emperor Brihadratha was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE.
Later Mauryas: Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha.
Causes: Brahmanical reaction, financial crisis, oppressive provincial rule.
Also: diffusion of material knowledge and neglect of the North-West frontier.
items.mnemonic: Decline causes 'BFONS' — Brahmanical reaction, Financial crisis, Oppression, New knowledge, NW-frontier neglect.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Mauryan Empire (Genealogy; Decline of the Mauryan Empire)

items.title: For Mains — The Mauryan Empire
items.body:
## For Mains — The Mauryan Empire

**In one line:** For Mains (GS Paper-2, clause M2-1: Magadha, Mauryas and Ashoka's Dharma), the Mauryas are examined analytically — administration as a model state, Ashoka's Dhamma as statecraft, the richness of sources, and the causes of decline.

### Dimensions Mains asks
| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Administration | Centralised autocracy; council; tirthas; revenue/justice officers; provinces; Pataliputra's six committees; espionage |
| Ashoka's Dhamma | Moral governance, paternal kingship, welfare; not a sect; critique that pacifism weakened the state |
| Sources | Arthashastra, Indica, Mudrarakshasa, 39 edicts, archaeology (NBPW, coins) — and their limits |
| Significance | First unification of India; model bureaucracy; ethics in governance |
| Decline | Brahmanical reaction, financial strain, oppression, knowledge diffusion, frontier neglect |
| Way forward / relevance | Ashokan "Dhamma" as a template for ethical, welfare-oriented governance |

### Data points / authorities to quote
- **Pliny:** army of 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 elephants — scale of the state.
- **Megasthenes' Indica:** six committees of five members ran Pataliputra.
- **Arthashastra:** 15 books, 180 chapters; Yogakshema (welfare) as the king's duty.
- **13th Major Rock Edict (261 BCE):** Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse.
- **R.S. Sharma / Romila Thapar:** decline as multi-causal (economic-religious strain plus over-centralisation).

### The AP angle
- **Erragudi (Yerragudi), Kurnool district** carries Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts, and **Rajula-Mandagiri** the Minor Rock Edicts — concrete proof that Mauryan Dhamma reached Andhra; use them to localise an answer on Ashoka's outreach.

### Use in answers
- **Example:** cite Erragudi (AP) to show the empire's southern reach.
- **Quote:** the Kalinga Edict — "All men are my children" — for paternal kingship.
- **Diagram idea:** a flow arrow "Bherighosha → Dhammaghosha" to show the policy shift; or a map of edict sites.
keyPoints: Mains clause M2-1 (GS Paper-2): Magadha, Mauryas and Ashoka's Dharma — treat analytically, not as a fact list.
Four exam angles: administration as a model state, Dhamma as statecraft, wealth of sources, multi-causal decline.
Quote data: Pliny's army figures, Megasthenes' six committees, Arthashastra (15 books/180 chapters, Yogakshema), 13th Rock Edict.
AP angle: Erragudi Major Rock Edicts and Rajula-Mandagiri Minor Rock Edicts localise Ashoka's Dhamma in Andhra.
Balance praise with critique: pacifism and anti-sacrifice policy are cited among causes of decline.
Use the Kalinga Edict quote ('All men are my children') and a Bherighosha → Dhammaghosha diagram.
